sections.title: Course Overview & the Central Argument

blocks.t: Course title: ‘Foresight, industrial strategy and digital policies: a new consistent trio in the EU’ — European Political and Governance Studies, Academic Year 2025-2026. Professor: Dimitri LORENZANI; Academic Assistant: Marco NICOLICH. It is an optional course (25h of teaching).

The central claim of the course: digitalisation is not merely a sectoral agenda — it has become a foundation for competitiveness, open strategic autonomy, economic security, regulation, the green transition and the fair transition.

“Industrial strategies today – as seen in the US and China – combine multiple policies, ranging from fiscal policies to encourage domestic production, to trade policies to penalise anti-competitive behaviour, to foreign economic policies to secure supply chains. In the EU context, linking policies in this way requires […] a new industrial strategy for Europe.” — Mario Draghi, ‘The Future of European Competitiveness’, September 2024

Dynamic policy coherence: the capacity to exploit synergies and assuage trade-offs with other policies over an inter-temporal setting — for instance ensuring that the pursued digital transition also interacts with the green and fair transitions as well as with the overarching goal of achieving Europe’s open strategic autonomy in an increasingly contested global arena.
The key takeaway of the course: Europe’s new industrial strategy, strategic foresight and digital laws/policies can be regarded as a new — and crucial — ‘consistent trio’ in EU policymaking.

items: Strategic foresight is the analytical lens (it anticipates risks, opportunities and dependencies).
Industrial strategy is the capacity-building agenda (it selects priorities).
Digital policy is both the object and the instrument of transformation (it supplies the regulatory and technological tools).

blocks.t: The course consists of 4 modules: (1) strategic foresight as a beacon of the EU’s new industrial strategy; (2) digitalisation and advanced technologies as a leg of Europe’s new industrial strategy and open strategic autonomy; (3) the EU as a digital normative superpower (regulatory); (4) dynamic coherence of the digital transition with the green/fair transition.

terms.d: Foresight + industrial strategy + digital policy as a new, crucial trio in EU policymaking.
The capacity to exploit synergies and manage trade-offs between policies over time, especially between digital, green, fair and security objectives.

sections.title: Digital Glossary (I): AI, Connectivity & Computing

blocks.t: Artificial intelligence (AI): the ability of a computer or computer-controlled robot to perform tasks associated with intelligent beings — reasoning, discovering meaning, generalizing, learning from past experience. It combines computer science and data analytics and encompasses machine learning and deep learning (AI algorithms that create expert systems to make predictions or classifications based on input data).

5G/6G: fifth- and sixth-generation technology for wireless communications over cellular data networks; operating on higher radio frequencies than 4G, providing more bandwidth and lower latency at microsecond speeds. Wireless generations are standardized by the International Telecommunication Union.
Edge (computing): a distributed computing paradigm/architecture that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, in order to improve response times and save bandwidth.
Supercomputing: a type of high-performance computing (HPC) using computers with high computational capabilities (supercomputers) to process complex calculations and large volumes of data.
Quantum (computing): the use of quantum (physics) phenomena like superposition and entanglement to perform computation exponentially faster than classic (electrodynamics) computers, including HPCs.

Internet of Things (IoT): devices with sensors, processing ability, software and other technologies that connect and exchange data with other devices and systems over the Internet or other communications networks.
Cloud: networked computing facilities providing remote data storage and processing services via the internet.

terms.d: The ability of a computer/robot to perform tasks of intelligent beings; combines computer science and data analytics; encompasses machine learning and deep learning.
Fifth-/sixth-generation wireless tech; higher frequencies than 4G; more bandwidth, lower (microsecond) latency; standardised by the ITU.

sections.title: Digital Glossary (II): Exascale, Twins, Data Centres & AI Models

blocks.t: Exascale: a measure of supercomputer performance — computing systems capable of calculating at least “10¹⁸ IEEE 754 Double Precision (64-bit) operations (multiplications and/or additions) per second (exaFLOPS)”.

Digital twins: a digital model of an intended or actual real-world physical product, system or process (the ‘physical twin’) that serves as its indistinguishable digital counterpart for practical purposes: simulation, integration, testing, monitoring, maintenance.

Data Centres: a centralized facility where an organization’s IT operations and equipment are concentrated, serving critical functions related to storing, processing and disseminating data and applications. Enterprise on-premise data centres are hosted in the organization’s own facilities (e.g. for greater control over security and regulatory compliance). Cloud computing data centres house IT infrastructure resources for shared use by multiple customers via the Internet. Cloud providers sometimes maintain smaller edge data centers closer to customers for lower latency or data-intensive workloads like big-data analytics.

Edge cloud (or fog): cloud computing that occurs at the network edge (the point where data is exchanged between devices — computers, smartphones, sensors, IoT devices — and cloud services) instead of sending data back to a central data center or private cloud. Advantages: reducing data latency; maintaining high availability by processing data closer to the source (if one edge location fails, another nearby can take over); and reducing the risk of unauthorized access to sensitive data via public networks.

AI model: a program trained on a set of data to perform specific tasks like recognizing certain patterns or making certain decisions. It uses algorithms to learn from data and apply that learning to achieve pre-defined objectives, and can make predictions when provided with the necessary information. An AI language model is a program that can recognize and generate text based on the preceding words.

A digital counterpart of a real-world physical product/system/process used for simulation, testing, monitoring, maintenance.
Centralized facilities concentrating IT operations for storing, processing and disseminating data; can be on-premise, cloud or edge.
Cloud computing at the network edge; reduces latency, raises availability, reduces unauthorized-access risk.

blocks.t: Foresight is “the discipline of exploring, anticipating and shaping the future”. It is a set of qualitative and quantitative tools and methods to build a safe space to ask disruptive questions and use collective intelligence in a structured way to prepare for future developments/crises (Strategic Foresight Report, 2020).
Strategic foresight is a foresight-based political narrative, informing today’s policies/decision-making through: analysis of long-term (mega)trends, and short-term horizon scanning.
“You are not doing a good job if you are not attracting some incoming fire.” — Hillary Clinton (cited to convey that good foresight challenges the status quo).
The slide closes with a ‘Post Scriptum: What foresight is not’ — a reminder that foresight is not prediction/fortune-telling but structured preparation.

sections.title: The Foresight Commissioner & Open Strategic Autonomy

blocks.t: “We want to keep Europe at the forefront of the sustainability transition, leveraging our unique social market economy and global trade power. This will help strengthen Europe’s leadership in the world, and our ability to stand on our own while building strong partnerships with others: this is what we call Europe’s open strategic autonomy.” — Maroš Šefčovič, Executive Vice-President for the European Green Deal, Interinstitutional Relations and Foresight.

Open strategic autonomy (OSA): the EU objective of reducing harmful dependencies while remaining outward-looking and cooperative where possible — being ‘as open as possible, as autonomous as necessary’ (and, more recently, increasingly the other way round).
OSA is the geopolitical dimension of resilience: the freedom and capacity to act in the world in an increasingly contested and multipolar global order.

sections.title: Megatrends & Horizon Scanning

blocks.t: The Commission’s Megatrends Hub analyses 14 global megatrends from an EU perspective — a crucial methodology underlying the Commission’s Strategic Foresight Reports.
Megatrends: large-scale, long-term driving forces that are observable now and could have significant influence on the future, impacting most human activities, processes and perceptions.

Horizon scanning: the Commission keeps an eye on the horizon to anticipate future developments — especially in areas of disruptive change/innovation like digital. Horizon scanners from ESPAS identify ‘signs of change’, then validated as ‘weak signals’ and explored in terms of their future impact via ‘sense-making sessions’. Output: quarterly horizon scanning newsletters presented to the College.
Examples cited: the Horizon Scanning bulletins of Dec 2023 and Nov 2025 (HorizonScanning_ESPAS_06.pdf).

sections.title: Module 1 — Key Takeaways

blocks.lead: The four key takeaways of Module 1:
items: Strategic foresight is the analytical lens of this course.

The Strategic Foresight Reports and other foresight input guided the Commission’s geopolitical awakening via more policy coherence around the concepts of resilience, open strategic autonomy and sustainable competitiveness.

The EU’s industrial strategy is the area most affected by this shift, through a new focus on sustainable competitiveness and mitigation of excessive strategic dependencies, as shown by the new Competitiveness Compass for Europe.

The rest of the course investigates how specific pieces of EU (digital) laws and policies fit this framework — with a focus on innovation and security (Module 2), regulatory superpower (Module 3) and dynamic coherence vis-à-vis green and social aspects (Module 4).

sections.title: Module 2 — A New EU Digital Industrial Strategy

blocks.t: Module 2: a new EU digital industrial strategy and its geopolitical/geoeconomic relevance. Focus: the build-up and diffusion of advanced technologies.

blocks.lead: The three pillars of the new digital industrial strategy:
items: More tech foresight & security of supply (identify high-potential techs to invest in or secure supply chains). Example: Chips Act + Economic Security Doctrine.
State-of-the-art enablers: fast and secure connectivity infrastructure, HPC, spectrum, etc. Example: AI Gigafactories + Cybersecurity Act.
Forward-looking approach to diffuse AI and general-purpose techs across industrial sectors of strength (‘vertical AI use cases’). Example: Apply AI + Cloud & AI Development Act.

sections.title: The EU’s ‘Middle Technology Trap’

blocks.t: Middle technology trap: the EU specialises in mid-tech, mature industries (notably automotive) rather than the frontier digital/software sectors where the US (and increasingly others) lead — leaving Europe stuck in the middle of the value/technology ladder.

Top firms by market value illustrate the gap. US (2003 → 2012 → 2022): Ford/Pfizer/GM → Microsoft/Intel/Merck → Google, Meta, Microsoft (all software). EU (2003 → 2012 → 2022): Mercedes/Siemens/VW → VW/Mercedes/Bosch → VW, Mercedes, Bosch (all auto) (Science, research and innovation performance of the EU, 2024).
Evidence base: the European Innovation Scoreboard 2024.

terms.d: The EU's over-specialisation in mid-tech, mature sectors (e.g. automotive) instead of frontier digital/software, leaving it lagging at the technology frontier.

sections.title: The EU Chips Act — Three Pillars

blocks.t: EU Chips Act: an EU Regulation that entered into force in September 2023 — the leitmotiv of the President’s State of the Union address — providing a framework to raise the EU’s production share to 20% by 2030.

items: Pillar 1 — ‘Chips for Europe’ initiative: pilot lines for testing advanced chips (incl. quantum); a cloud-based electronic-design-automation (EDA) platform; chips competence centres in MS to boost skills; a Chips Fund (3.3 bn EUR from Horizon Europe & Digital Europe Programme, blended under InvestEU & EIC) to catalyse 43 bn EUR public/private investment by 2030.

Pillar 2 — Security of supply and resilience: FOAK (first-of-a-kind) integrated production facilities (IPF) & open EU foundries (OEF) ‘of public interest’ can access financial aid and admin support (e.g. fast construction permits); Design Centres of Excellence.

Pillar 3 — Monitoring and crisis response: a European Semiconductor Board (ESB) supports the Commission in strategic mapping and monitoring (incl. preventive measures if national authorities alert COM); an emergency toolbox (QMV in Council) if serious disruptions affect a critical sector: (1) information gathering from firms (enforced with fines); (2) priority-rated orders (last resort, after consulting ESB); (3) common purchasing of crisis-related products.

terms.d: EU Regulation (in force Sept 2023) to raise the EU chip production share to 20% by 2030; 3 pillars: Chips for Europe; security of supply; monitoring/crisis response.
Supports the Commission in strategic mapping/monitoring of chips and is consulted before priority-rated orders.

sections.title: Bespoke State Aid & the ‘Chips Subsidies Race’

blocks.t: EU state-aid rules allow targeted support for chips R&D but not manufacturing; moreover, IPCEIs are complex and lengthy (up to 3 years) — e.g. the 2nd IPCEI on Microelectronics and Communication Technologies (June 2023).

The Chips Act introduced a bespoke State aid approach for chips manufacturing: “Commission recognizes the need for a case-by-case assessment, where public support includes State aid that does not fall under existing guidelines […] may be justified […] up to 100% of a proven funding gap, if such facilities would otherwise not exist in Europe.”

items: Criteria: FOAK; cross-border impact; supply security; funding-gap analysis.
Scale of the global race (announced/subsidy programmes): EU ~EUR 100 bn announced; US CHIPS and Science Act $53 bn (tax incentives, state grants); China $150–200 bn; Japan $5 bn.
Direction of travel: towards a Chips Act 2.0 in 2026.

sections.title: Security Dimension — the ‘Chips War’

blocks.t: The EU Chips Act is an example of efforts towards a new EU industrial policy for critical tech inputs like semiconductors (more domestic capacities & more secure supply from third countries).

Battle of narratives, offers and models (2023 SFR): EU tech sovereignty helps fight a battle on the global stage and is key for security & defence (a stronger Europe in the world) and EU values (a Europe that protects), vis-à-vis: third countries’ propaganda amplified by social media/AI; and third countries’ alternative offers to the EU Global Gateway or the Partnership for Global Infrastructure & Investment (e.g. China’s Belt and Road Initiative and Digital Silk Road).
Securing critical digital infrastructure matters for global influence and for the ‘battle of models’ between democratic and authoritarian regimes.

sections.title: Economic Security Strategy — the 3 P’s

blocks.t: Economic Security Strategy (2023 Communication): a new comprehensive (country-agnostic?) approach to risk management built on the 3 P’s — promoting competitiveness, protecting economic security, partnering with like-minded countries (…and Preparing?) — to jointly assess and minimise risks related to: supply-chain resilience; physical and cyber security of critical infrastructure; technology security and leakage; and the weaponisation of dependencies and economic coercion.

Tool-testing & evidence-building (2023-2025): a recommendation lists 10 critical technologies for risk mitigation and flags 4 high-risk areas (advanced chips, AI, quantum, biotech) for immediate joint risk assessment and evaluation of the need for restrictive measures or support (under STEP). Complemented by pilots on FDI screening, export controls and outbound investments.

sections.title: The Economic Security Doctrine (Dec 2025)

blocks.lead: Operationalisation with the December 2025 Economic Security Doctrine:
items: Tighter FDI Screening: a 2024 Regulation to create conformity in inbound investment screening (minimum sectoral scope, extended targets, all MS with a screening regime).
Coordination among MS’ export controls, against unilateral measures and based on common EU lists (2024 White Paper).
Outbound Investments screening: a 2025 Recommendation to avoid circumvention of export controls and leakage.

Scale up dual-use / advanced-tech R&D and prevent technology leakage: tailoring cross-sector EU programmes to finance it (linking the EU Chips Act with Horizon) and boosting research security vis-à-vis third countries (including a new EU Centre).

blocks.t: The Doctrine makes these standard components of an EU economic-security governance, classified in 6 high-risk areas, tied to risk thresholds, and thus normalised and scalable.

sections.title: The EU Cybersecurity Acquis

blocks.lead: Three pillars of the cybersecurity acquis:
items: NIS2 Directive
Cybersecurity Act
Cyber Resilience Act (+ sectoral acts and a cyber-diplomacy toolbox)

blocks.t: NIS2: a mechanism of EU-wide cooperation on the cyber-security of critical infrastructure (network and information systems for essential and important entities) with harmonised requirements (e.g. cyber-risk management, business continuity, reporting to national authorities) and fines up to 2% of turnover otherwise. Essential entities include energy, healthcare, public sector, banking, transport, digital infrastructure (and submarine cables under certain conditions). Important entities include digital service providers, food production and waste management — a whole-of-supply-chain/systemic approach.

Cyber Resilience Act (CRA): a regulation introducing mandatory cybersecurity requirements for manufacturers throughout the product lifecycle. Compliance (acknowledged via CE marking) is required for EU market access (from 2027) and enforced with fines up to EUR 15 mn or 2.5% of turnover.

EU Cybersecurity Act: a regulation on a voluntary EU cybersecurity certification for products, services and processes. Certificates are recognised in all MS and encourage security-by-design, making cross-border trade easier — cybersecurity becomes a competitive advantage for EU industry. It gives a permanent mandate to ENISA and creates a new EU Cybersecurity Competence Centre (ECCC) in Bucharest to ensure MS synergies.

terms.d: EU-wide cooperation on cybersecurity of critical infrastructure; harmonised requirements for essential and important entities; fines up to 2% of turnover.
Mandatory lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for manufacturers; CE marking; EU market access from 2027; fines up to €15mn or 2.5% turnover.
Voluntary EU cybersecurity certification scheme; security-by-design; permanent ENISA mandate; ECCC in Bucharest.
The EU Agency for Cybersecurity, given a permanent mandate by the Cybersecurity Act.

blocks.t: The EU’s technological sovereignty is challenged by the weaponisation of interdependence by third countries, relevant for critical digital infrastructure.
China’s HMN constructed and upgraded undersea cables connecting Member States and Indo-Pacific areas with NATO military bases.

The US banned Huawei’s equipment and prohibited TikTok on government devices. In the EU: 14 MS have no restrictions on high-risk suppliers; only EU institutions and a few MS banned TikTok on government devices.

sections.title: Module 2 — Key Takeaways

blocks.lead: The four key takeaways of Module 2:
items: The EU needs a new digital industrial policy focused on open strategic autonomy, combining R&I and industrial policies to exit its middle technology trap.

A new digital industrial policy should leverage at the same time investments and regulation, with three pillars: (i) technology horizon scanning & economic security; (ii) cyber-secure digital infrastructure; and (iii) vertical AI use cases.
This strategy has clear geopolitical and security implications — contributing to a ‘battle of narratives, offers and models’ on the global stage.

Regulatory milestones include: (i) the EU Chips Act and Economic Security Strategy; (ii) the EU cyber-security framework; and (iii) the inter-linked components of the AI Continent Strategy (e.g. AI Gigafactories initiative and steps towards an EU cloud/edge).

terms.d: The umbrella linking AI Gigafactories, EU cloud/edge steps and related initiatives as part of the new digital industrial policy.

sections.title: Module 3 — The EU as a Digital Normative Superpower?

blocks.t: Normative power / normative superpower: influence based on rules, values and standards rather than military or purely economic coercion. The EU can project power through law by setting binding standards.
Brussels effect: the EU’s capacity to shape global markets through regulation, because firms adapt to EU rules and sometimes diffuse those standards beyond Europe.

blocks.lead: The SFRs build the standard-setting case:
items: 2021 SFR: ensuring a first-mover position in standard setting.
2022 SFR: a strategic approach to influencing international standardisation, e.g. in batteries.
2023 SFR: a transatlantic marketplace, also in digital standards.

blocks.t: Digital: pioneering regulations (e.g. the AI Act) for a more human-centric digital transition “have influenced the evolution of the global regulatory framework”. In a global battle of narratives, offers and models, other geo-blocks take assertive standard-setting actions (e.g. China Standards 2035), and ‘Digital Empires’ governance models are evolving or fighting for influence.

sections.title: Digital Empires & the Battles for Influence

blocks.t: Digital Empires (Anu Bradford): a ‘horizontal battle’ for influence (‘regulatory un-peace’) between three governance models. (1) US market-driven model: regulation handed over to tech companies to maximise innovation. (2) China’s state-driven model: authoritarian control enabled by tech-based tools but open to economic interdependence. (3) EU rights-driven model: boosted by economic size.
There is also a ‘vertical battle’ for influence: governments vs tech giants.

Intersections: acquiescence for economic interest; the need for international techno-democratic regulatory cooperation to meet public opinion’s shift away from trust in market self-regulation; and the question of whether the EU is the only credible techno-democratic alternative offer to China’s.

terms.d: Anu Bradford's framing of three rival digital-governance models (US market-driven, China state-driven, EU rights-driven).

sections.title: Linking Foresight & Regulation — Agile Regulatory Tools

blocks.t: Andrea Renda maps regulatory tools by phase of the ‘policy cycle’ (with maturity, government-capacity requirements and innovation impact).

items: Agenda-setting: crowdsourcing priorities; horizon scanning & strategic foresight; transition pathways and backcasting.
Regulatory: self- and co-regulation & outcome-based regulation; regulatory sandboxes (+ testbeds, policy experiments, innovation deals/hubs); tech sprints and regulatory hackathons.
Implementation/enforcement: regulatory guidance to support compliance; RegTech and SupTech, predictive analytics; innovation hubs.

blocks.t: Regulatory sandbox: a controlled scheme (under an ‘experimentation clause’) where applicants are screened and tested; results are evaluated for suitability, scalability, representativeness and reliability before deployment/authorisation (or the sandbox ‘fails’).

terms.d: A controlled testing scheme under an experimentation clause; screens applicants, evaluates results before authorisation.

sections.title: Example of a Regulatory Sandbox — Open Banking

blocks.t: The UK’s sandbox for open banking was launched in 2016 by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) — one of the first of its kind globally.
Many tested solutions went to market (e.g. Open Banking apps) and other jurisdictions adopted a similar model based on the UK (and the EU’s PSD2) experience.

Process flow: an experimentation clause → sandbox screening of applicants → evaluation (suitability, scalability, representativeness, reliability) → if results are sufficiently robust and positive and residual risks are managed with real-world safeguards, the firm exits to authorisation/deployment; otherwise the application is rejected or the sandbox ‘failed’.

terms.d: The UK FCA's 2016 sandbox (one of the first globally); influenced other jurisdictions alongside the EU's PSD2.
The EU's revised Payment Services Directive, part of the open-banking experience referenced in the sandbox example.

sections.title: The AI Act — Normative Superpower in Digital?

blocks.t: AI Act: the world’s first horizontal regulation on AI — a common binding framework for the use & supply of AI systems in the EU; Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. A clear example of a rights-based normative superpower (with echoes in the US, China, UK and beyond).

It is largely a risk-based and precautionary approach, but offers good examples of agile / experimental / adaptive regulation: co-regulation, compulsory regulatory sandboxes, and guidance for compliance.

The AI Pact seeks industry’s voluntary pledges to anticipate AI Act provisions (over 100 in Sep 2024; over 230 in Jan 2026); voluntary codes of conduct for non-high-risk AI systems; EU harmonised standards for presumption of conformity; and pilot sandboxes in the MS since 2022 (ES — Spain).

terms.d: World's first horizontal AI regulation, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; rights-based, risk-based, with agile tools (sandboxes, codes, guidance).
Voluntary industry pledges to anticipate AI Act provisions (100+ in Sep 2024, 230+ in Jan 2026).

options: the world's first horizontal regulation on AI
quiz.source: World’s first horizontal regulation on AI: common binding framework for use & supply of AI systems in EU.

quiz.source: Artificial Intelligence Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689.

quiz.source: pilot sandboxes in the MS since 2022 (ES).

sections.title: The AI Act — Risk-Based Architecture

blocks.t: The AI Act applies to all providers placing AI systems and GPAI models on the EU market (with exceptions such as military).

Risk-based approach: a ban for 8 unacceptable-risk systems; strong requirements (e.g. conformity assessment) on high-risk ones; transparency obligations on low-risk ones; and minimal obligations otherwise.

Enforcement is phased, with an attempt to move it forward via the AI Pact with firms. There are special provisions for GPAI models (presumption of conformity via standards), and regulatory sandboxes are mandated at MS level to test innovative solutions.

terms.d: Unacceptable (8 banned), high-risk (conformity assessment), low-risk (transparency), minimal (minimal obligations).
The strong compliance requirement imposed on high-risk AI systems.

quiz.q: The AI Act bans how many 'unacceptable-risk' AI practices? ______
quiz.source: Risk-based approach: ban for 8 unacceptable-risk ones.

options: strong requirements such as conformity assessment
quiz.source: strong requirements (e.g. conformity assessment) on high-risk ones.

quiz.q: Low-risk AI systems are subject mainly to…
quiz.source: transparency obligations on low-risk ones; minimal obligations otherwise.

sections.title: The AI Act — GPAI, Sandboxing & Governance

items: Vast transparency requirements for all GPAI models.
Special provisions for GPAI models with high-impact capabilities (presumption of posing systemic risks): notification, risk assessment and mitigation.
Codes of practice by the Commission and presumption of conformity for compliance with EU harmonised standards (agile regulation).
National authorities must establish at least one regulatory sandbox at national level to facilitate development and testing of innovative AI systems.
Prospective providers of high-risk AI systems may test them in advance in real-world conditions if they respect guarantees (e.g. asking for consent).

blocks.t: Governance & fines: MS must designate at least a market surveillance authority and a notifying authority. Fines up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (whichever is higher) for infringements on prohibited practices or non-compliance on data (lower fines for smaller companies). EU-level actors: the Commission (implementing/delegated acts, oversight of standardisation), the AI Board, the AI Office and EU standardisation bodies.

The 2025 Digital Omnibus (under negotiation) extends compliance deadlines: currently 02/12/27 for listed high-risk AI systems (e.g. employment, law enforcement, education) and 02/12/28 for AI systems embedded in regulated products (e.g. medical devices, machinery).

terms.d: General-purpose AI models; all face transparency requirements; high-impact ones presumed to pose systemic risks (notification, risk assessment, mitigation).
Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (whichever higher) for the gravest infringements.
Under negotiation; extends AI Act compliance deadlines (02/12/27 for listed high-risk; 02/12/28 for AI in regulated products).

sections.title: Module 3 — Key Takeaways

items: Key digital regulation across the ‘pillars’ of the Digital Single Market (AI Act, DMA, DSA, etc.) is an area where the EU can still claim a ‘normative superpower’ status — e.g. via standardisation practices contributing to ‘functional’ sovereignty (and thus OSA) within the Digital Empires’ horizontal and vertical battles for influence.

Despite large and persistent regulatory divergences, moving towards a ‘digital transatlantic marketplace’ via more EU-US (and beyond) regulatory compatibility and cooperation would respond to such geo-economic interests.

Agile regulatory tools — including strategic foresight and private-sector involvement (co-regulation, standardisation, regulatory sandboxes) — also contribute to these strategic goals and are part of a new digital industrial policy.

terms.d: The EU project of integrating digital markets, reducing fragmentation and creating common rules for online services and digital business.

sections.title: Module 4 — Dynamic Coherence of the Digital with the Green/Fair Transition

blocks.t: Module 4: the dynamic coherence of the digital transition with the green/fair transition — pairing, as in the SFRs, a JRC ‘Science for Policy Report’ with a Commission Communication.
Core question: can the digital transition reinforce the green and fair transitions rather than undermine them? Dynamic coherence asks whether policy can manage these interdependencies over time.

terms.d: The combined green and digital transition; managing synergies and trade-offs between them over time.

quiz.q: Module 4's central concept for managing green-digital interdependencies over time is…
quiz.source: Dynamic coherence asks whether policy can manage these interdependencies over time.

sections.title: Solving the EU’s Industrial-Policy Trilemma

blocks.t: Industrial-policy trilemma (Renda, 2024): the tension between competitiveness, decarbonisation and economic security — and, adding fairness, a quadrilemma — that industrial policy must manage.
Digitalisation can help solve / assuage the trilemma/quadrilemma by exploiting synergies and reducing trade-offs across these overlapping (and sometimes competing) goals.

terms.d: The tension between competitiveness, decarbonisation, economic security (trilemma) plus fairness (quadrilemma) that industrial policy must manage (Renda, 2024).

quiz.q: The industrial-policy trilemma (Renda) is between competitiveness, decarbonisation and…
quiz.source: Solving the EU’s industrial policy trilemma… competitiveness and decarbonization (Source: Andrea Renda, 2024).

quiz.source: industrial policy trilemma / quadrilemma between economic security, competitiveness and decarbonization, plus fairness.

sections.title: 2022 SFR — Tech Factors to Assuage Trade-offs

blocks.t: The 2022 SFR identifies digital technology factors to assuage green-digital trade-offs, including: digital technologies for sustainable farming; environmental monitoring systems; reduced demand for space; building design and redesign; self-organised microgrids & grid-based governance of the e-system; energy-as-a-service; materials optimisation (via AI); materials and wastes tracing; Mobility as a Service (MaaS)/Transport as a Service (TaaS); and digital twins.

sections.title: Twinning by 2050 — a Scenario-Based Approach

blocks.t: Understanding forward-looking interplays between the digital and green/fair transition can reduce trade-offs and maximise synergies.
Key figures: ICT is responsible for 7%–9% of global electricity use (a trade-off); AI-based systems could reduce global emissions by 4% (a synergy).
The JRC built 4 scenarios of a sustainable Europe in 2050 along 2 axes: societal behaviour (individualistic vs collaborative) and policy mix (less vs more supportive of sustainability).
Equity dimension: the analysis covers green and social factors — e.g. the richest decile emits 3 times more per capita than all other citizens.

terms.d: JRC scenarios of a sustainable Europe in 2050 along two axes: societal behaviour (individualistic vs collaborative) and policy mix (less vs more supportive of sustainability).

quiz.source: ICT responsible of 7%-9% of global electricity use.

quiz.source: the richest decile emits 3 times more per capita than all other citizens.

sections.title: From Scenarios to Policy Pathways

blocks.t: Green business boom: change is primarily driven by the market and by innovation. As resource costs surge, corporations decouple profits from resource consumption — engaging in the circular economy, renewable energies and sustainable bio-economy. Innovation accelerates market opportunities for sustainable business models (enabled by new digital techs), so the economy promotes sustainable behaviour while generating added value. This movement is global, as geopolitical conflicts in the 2020s generated a strong pushback.

Glocal eco-world: policymakers failed to respond effectively to the major havoc brought by climate change, forcing people to adapt to more difficult circumstances. Society shifts to a new paradigm: people (re)discover the value of human relationships, connections, community help and the possibility of a dignified life with lower levels of material prosperity.

terms.d: A 2050 scenario where market + innovation decouple profits from resource use (circular economy, renewables, bio-economy).
A 2050 scenario where, after failed policy responses to climate havoc, society adapts with lower material prosperity but stronger human relationships and community.

quiz.source: Green business boom: change is primarily driven by the market and by innovation.

options: policymakers failed to respond effectively to climate change
quiz.source: Glocal eco-world: policymakers failed to respond effectively to the major havoc brought by climate change.

sections.title: Industry 5.0 & Society 5.0

blocks.t: Industry 5.0: an approach that links industrial transformation with human-centricity, sustainability and resilience — (digital) technologies for the SDGs.

Society 5.0: a ‘super-smart industrial transformation and society’ combining broad societal goals like the SDGs with new technologies. Innovation is useful as it enables addressing global societal challenges.

A 'super-smart' society combining societal goals (SDGs) with new technologies.

sections.title: Example — AI in Healthcare

blocks.t: AI has a key ‘vertical’ application to healthcare throughout the lifecycle of medicinal products: (1) speeding up (efficiency gains) the discovery of novel compounds with potential medicinal applications; (2) rapidly identifying patients for phase III clinical trials; (3) personalising therapies & optimising treatment plans.
Key use case for COVID-19 vaccines: the EU-funded project Exscalate used HPC to screen molecules.

blocks.lead: Advantages of HPC & AI to accelerate drug discovery (down from the current 9.1 years for clinical development):
items: More effective patent protection (and a larger market).
Large cost savings (up to 50%) with some pass-through.

terms.d: EU-funded project that used HPC to screen molecules — a key AI/HPC use case for COVID-19 vaccines.

quiz.source: Key use case for COVID-19 vaccines (EU-funded project Exscalate used HPC to screen molecules).

quiz.source: Large cost savings (up to 50%) with some pass-through.

sections.title: The Technology/Jobs Puzzle

blocks.t: Technology/jobs puzzle: the AI revolution will transform the job market — but will it lead to job loss? Productivity growth and job expansion could be another outcome (example: preventive medicine), but how to achieve it? The issue is not only numerical: policymakers should create ‘good jobs’ in ‘good sectors’.

Skills foresight across key industrial ecosystems can empower workers along the digital transition and boost innovation — e.g. Industry 5.0, the Pact for Skills, the Alliance for Apprenticeships, the New Innovation Agenda, Deep Tech Talent Initiatives, Net-Zero Academies.

items: Industrial policy meets (skills) foresight to veer towards the creation of needed skills in sectors deemed strategic.
A common space for skills as part of a digital transatlantic (or transpacific) marketplace.

terms.d: Whether the AI revolution causes job loss or job expansion; the goal is 'good jobs' in 'good sectors' via skills foresight (Renda, Balland, Bosoer 2023).
Anticipating skills needs across industrial ecosystems to empower workers and boost innovation.

sections.title: Digital Skills — the Digital Decade Targets

blocks.t: 42-44% of Europeans do not have basic digital skills (particularly older people and rural areas), hampering everyday tasks and access to online services — this means less than 70%, against the 2030 target of 80%.
The skills gap (by age, gender, education, urbanisation) is large and varies across Member States.

ICT specialists in the EU (81% of which are male) increased by 57.8% in 2012-2022 but are still flagged as insufficient by 85% of EU firms. The status quo would mean just 12 million ICT specialists by 2030 — well below the 20 million Digital Decade target.

terms.d: 80% of people with basic digital skills and 20 million ICT specialists by 2030; the EU currently lags both.

quiz.source: less than 70% of the 2030 target of 80%.

quiz.source: well below the 20 million DD target.

quiz.source: 42-44% of Europeans do not have basic digital skills.

sections.title: A New EU Social Contract — Gig Workers

blocks.t: The gig economy and platform work are rising: 28 mn gig workers in 2022, 43 mn in 2025.
Issue: 93% (26 mn) of workers are classified as self-employed, not entitled to the same rights & protection as employees. Around 5 million (19%) are likely to be incorrectly classified.

The EU is the 1st legislator in the world to regulate platform work: the Council adopted the Platform Work Directive in October 2024. Member States have 2 years to transpose it. It (1) helps determine the correct employment status & social protection (self-employed vs employees); and (2) establishes rules on the use of algorithms in the workplace and related transparency safeguards.

terms.d: Adopted by the Council in October 2024; the EU is the first legislator worldwide to regulate platform work; MS have 2 years to transpose.

quiz.source: 28 mn gig workers in 2022, 43 mn in 2025.

quiz.source: 93% (26 mn) of workers are classified as self-employed.

sections.title: Platform Work Directive — Mechanisms

items: A rebuttable legal presumption of employment relationship based on control/direction elements in national law or collective agreement in force, with modalities set out by each Member State.
Use of algorithms in the workplace: workers to be informed about automated monitoring & decision-making; personal data protected; human oversight at least for significant decisions.
Enforcement of transparency & traceability: platforms to declare work to national authorities (including cross-border).

blocks.t: The debate on control triggers is complex: sometimes platforms’ rate control is to the workers’ advantage or to users’ benefit (certainty).

terms.d: The Platform Work Directive's mechanism: workers presumed employees based on control/direction elements, unless rebutted; modalities set by each MS.

sections.title: Module 4 — Key Takeaways

blocks.lead: The four key takeaways of Module 4:
items: Digitalisation can help solve the industrial-policy trilemma/quadrilemma between economic security, competitiveness and decarbonisation, plus fairness, as overlapping (and sometimes competing) goals.
Twinning mainstreaming is evident across EU policymaking — from the Digital Decade’s focus on climate-neutral data centres and low-energy semiconductors to the Critical Raw Materials Act.

Skills foresight across key industrial ecosystems can assuage the technology/jobs puzzle, helping move towards ‘good jobs’ in ‘good (strategic) sectors’. Skills foresight and a focus on digital skills are part of the 2025 Union of Skills strategy.
A new (digital) industrial strategy for Europe also calls for a new EU social contract, including adequate workers’ protection in the digital world (the Platform Work Directive).

terms.d: Cited as evidence of twinning mainstreaming across EU policymaking.
The 2025 strategy of which skills foresight and digital skills are a part.

quiz.q: Twinning mainstreaming is illustrated by the Digital Decade's focus on climate-neutral data centres and…
quiz.source: from the Digital Decade’s focus on climate-neutral data centres and low-energy semiconductors, to the Critical Raw Materials Act.

quiz.source: Skills foresight and a focus on digital skills are part of the 2025 Union of Skills strategy.

sections.title: The DSA & DMA — the ‘Digital (not twin) Sisters’

blocks.t: The DSA and DMA are recent Regulations. The DSA ensures a safer digital space where average users’ fundamental rights are protected (especially vis-à-vis VLOPs — very large online platforms). The DMA ensures a level playing field for businesses (e.g. SMEs, start-ups) and a fair choice for business users marketing products/services online, vis-à-vis gatekeepers.

Digital technologies create new ways to exercise and infringe fundamental rights and freedoms (the ‘battle of models’) — e.g. trade of illegal content online, disinformation, and private rule-makers in digital markets. The DSA/DMA mark the start of a long, collaborative process to change the status quo.

terms.d: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on online intermediary services: due-diligence obligations, systemic risks and platform accountability; protects users' fundamental rights, esp. vis-à-vis VLOPs.
Regulation imposing obligations on gatekeeper platforms to promote contestability and fairness; protects a level playing field for business users.
Very Large Online Platforms — the focus of the DSA's strongest obligations.
Large platforms subject to DMA obligations to ensure contestability and fairness.

options: users' fundamental rights and a safer digital space (esp. vs VLOPs)
a level playing field for businesses vs gatekeepers
quiz.source: safer digital space where average users’ fundamental rights are protected (DSA) especially vis-à-vis VLOPs.

quiz.q: The DMA primarily targets…
options: gatekeepers, to ensure contestability and a level playing field
quiz.source: a level playing field for businesses… vis-à-vis gatekeepers online (DMA).

sections.title: Origins, Due Diligence & Gatekeeper Obligations

blocks.t: Origins in e-commerce law: the 2000 E-commerce Directive is the origin point for EU intermediary-liability and digital-services rules; the regulatory landscape also includes the 2018 Audiovisual Media Services Directive update.

DSA — asymmetric due diligence: obligations scale with the size and systemic role of the service. The DSA imposes due-diligence obligations, addresses systemic risks and establishes platform accountability, with the heaviest duties on the largest platforms (VLOPs).

DMA — gatekeeper obligations: the DMA imposes ex ante obligations on gatekeeper platforms to promote contestability and fairness (e.g. against self-preferencing and unfair conditions for business users).
Official citations from the reading list: Digital Services Act, Regulation (EU) 2022/2065; the DSA/DMA are presented in depth in the Filomena Chirico seminar.

terms.d: The origin point for EU intermediary-liability and digital-services rules.
DSA obligations scale with the size and systemic role of the service; heaviest on VLOPs.

sections.title: A Shield for Europe — Reviving the European Defence Community

blocks.t: ‘A Shield for Europe: Reviving the European Defence Community’ (Federico Fabbrini, Survival, 2025, 67:1, 55-60). A defence-policy reading on European security, OSA and the potential revival of an EDC-like framework.

Context: a major conventional inter-state war returned to Europe (Russia’s aggression against Ukraine); EU leaders called it a ‘tectonic shift in European history’ in the Versailles Declaration of March 2022; Trump’s re-election compounds the challenge. If the US withheld support, the EU would become, by default, the main instrument of European defence solidarity.

European Defence Community (EDC): in 1951 six countries — Belgium, France, Italy, Luxembourg, the Netherlands and West Germany — founded the ECSC with the 1951 Treaty of Paris; in 1952 they established the EDC, explicitly focused on defending Western Europe (France also saw it as a way to deal with the remilitarisation of Germany).

Fabbrini argues that since the four states that ratified it never rescinded their ratification, if France and Italy approved the treaty today, the EDC would become operational; the EDC would be interconnected with NATO (allaying decoupling fears), open to any EU state (with a veto on uncooperative partners), and would build a bridge with the UK.

terms.d: A 1950s supranational defence framework (est. 1952), revisited by Fabbrini (2025) as a possible model for European defence solidarity.
EU leaders called Russia's war a 'tectonic shift in European history'.
Founded the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) by six countries.

sections.title: Oral Presentation Themes (the Five Debates)

blocks.lead: The course treats five policy debates as central:
items: Group 1: the links (synergies and trade-offs) between European industrial policy and competition policy — with a focus on the digital field; present at least 2 recent examples of EU digital legislation where this tension is most relevant.
Group 2: the pros and cons of tech export controls and preference clauses in trade/public procurement — are they necessary for economic security or the end of Europe’s openness?
Group 3: the pros and cons of Europe’s (over)regulating the digital world — the balance between the principle of precaution and innovation; present 2 recent examples and compare with the AI Act.
Group 4: the pros and cons of alternative strategies to make the digital transition greener (innovation-led vs de-growth strategies towards decarbonisation; best achieving the twinning).
Group 5: the new ‘socio-economic models’ imposed by digitalisation (labour market, skills, inequalities) — ‘How can digitalisation be part of the solution rather than of the problem?’

sections.title: Thematic Synthesis — Five Cross-Cutting Themes

blocks.t: 1. The consistent trio: digital policy must be embedded in a broader industrial and foresight strategy. Foresight identifies long-term risks and scenarios; industrial strategy selects capacity-building priorities; digital policy supplies the regulatory and technological instruments.

2. Open strategic autonomy & economic security: building capacity and reducing excessive dependencies without simply closing the EU economy; reframing supply chains, critical technologies, cybersecurity and infrastructure as risk-management fields.

3. The EU as digital normative superpower: projecting power through law by setting binding standards (AI, platforms, services, gatekeepers); linked to the Brussels effect and global regulatory competition.

4. Dynamic policy coherence & the twin/fair transition: digitalisation creates both opportunities and trade-offs for decarbonisation and social fairness; coherence manages these interdependencies over time.

5. Competitiveness, productivity & the innovation lifecycle: competitiveness is connected to digital innovation, scale-up capacity, R&I, skills and industrial ecosystems; the EU must escape a middle-technology trap.

sections.title: Exam Preparation — Topics, Pitfalls & Model Plans

items: The consistent trio as the EU’s new policy paradigm.
Open strategic autonomy in digital technologies.

The EU competitiveness problem and the role of digital industrial policy.
Digitalisation, decarbonisation and fairness: solving the industrial-policy trilemma.
Define strategic foresight; define open strategic autonomy; define the Brussels effect.

What is the EU Chips Act designed to address? What is dynamic policy coherence?
How does the AI Act structure regulation by risk? What is the technology/jobs puzzle?

blocks.t: Common mistakes to avoid: treating digital policy as only market regulation (ignoring industrial capacity); using OSA as a synonym for protectionism; describing the AI Act/DSA/DMA without explaining their different regulatory logics; listing instruments without linking them to competitiveness/autonomy/coherence; ignoring trade-offs (innovation vs regulation; openness vs security; digitalisation vs jobs; green transition vs industrial cost).

High-value arguments: foresight is the analytical lens, industrial strategy the capacity-building agenda, digital policy both object and instrument; the EU’s regulatory strength must be connected to innovation and scale-up; OSA is about managing dependencies, not withdrawing; green and digital transitions are not automatically coherent — policy must create synergies; structure answers as concept → policy example → trade-off → conclusion.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Swinging Moment & the Four ‘Shorings’

blocks.t: The Von der Leyen I (VDL 1) Commission was a swinging moment in EU industrial policy. Recent history shows a cyclical pattern (the slide evokes Vico’s 18th-century idea that history repeats itself) between vertical policy (defending a specific sector or champion) and horizontal policy (non-sector-specific framework rules on credit, education, financing). The shift tracks liberalisation vs protectionist waves.

VDL 1 marks an acceleration of the shift under way since the 2008 crisis — from a horizontal model towards a more vertical, interventionist, sector-specific model (open strategic autonomy). The narrative: (i) reduce strategic dependencies, especially on the US and China; (ii) boost industrial capacities; and (iii) resort to ‘shoring’ strategies.

The four ‘shoring’ practices: Onshoring — a company without offshore production increases national production that did not exist before. Reshoring — bringing back operations set up abroad to the domestic market (for security, supply-chain resilience, domestic capacity, IP protection, quality control, cost efficiency). Friendshoring — producing in allied countries. Nearshoring — locating production in directly neighbouring countries.

Origins of the strategy: in 2019, VDL 1’s industrial strategy had two pillars — the green and digital transitions. COVID (and the offshoring of medicine production to India) added a third pillar: resilience and the reduction of strategic dependencies, pursued mostly with financial instruments such as the EU budget / RRF (Recovery and Resilience Facility).

terms.d: A firm with no offshore production increasing national production that did not previously exist.
Bringing business operations set up abroad back to the domestic market (security, resilience, IP, quality, cost).
Producing in allied (like-minded) countries.
Locating production in directly neighbouring countries.
EU industrial policy swings cyclically between vertical (sector/champion-specific) and horizontal (economy-wide framework) models; VDL 1 accelerated the swing toward vertical.

quiz.source: Friendshoring: producing in ally countries.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Draghi Report — Three Pillars

blocks.lead: The Draghi Report (‘The Future of European Competitiveness’, Sept 2024) is built on three pillars:
items: Increasing security and reducing strategic dependencies.
Boosting the growth of green technologies.
Closing the innovation gap.

blocks.t: Innovation-based productivity is the fil rouge of the whole report — evidence that a ‘swinging moment’ has occurred.

The report makes 140 recommendations aimed at structural growth (demography, innovation…), as opposed to cyclical growth (short-term interest-rate, demand and trade variations). The EU faces massive investment needs — the IMF estimates ~€1 trillion of yearly investment to achieve the transitions.

A blunt conclusion of the report: without a new industrial strategy, the EU is ‘condemned to death by slow agony’. Other drivers of the shift: rising energy costs, falling external (trade) demand, and global political instability.

terms.d: (i) security/reduce dependencies; (ii) grow green technologies; (iii) close the innovation gap — with innovation-based productivity as the report's fil rouge.
Structural growth rests on demography and innovation; cyclical growth on short-term interest rates, shocks, trade and demand.

sections.title: Deep Dive · From Antwerp to Budapest — Building the Compass

blocks.t: Antwerp Declaration for a European Industrial Deal (February 2024): an initiative signed by over 1300 business organisations across 25 sectors, calling for a European Industrial Deal to boost industrial competitiveness and sustainability.

European Council Strategic Agenda 2024-2029 (June 2024): calls for industrial competitiveness, promotion of innovation and reduction of strategic dependencies — a first policy response, in line with Draghi.

Budapest Declaration on the New European Competitiveness Deal (informal European Council, November 2024): translates Draghi’s proposals into tools/goals — (i) simplification (a new omnibus targeting a −35% administrative burden for SMEs); (ii) a 28th regime for European companies (reducing burden and fragmentation); (iii) digital sovereignty (data cybersecurity, resilience of digital infrastructures).

The debate continues — e.g. the February 2026 European Council retreat in Brussels on industrial competitiveness. Von der Leyen points to key initiatives implementing Draghi: the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) and the Competitiveness Coordination Tool (CCT). Informal European Councils are held in the capital of the rotating presidency.

terms.d: Signed by 1300+ business organisations across 25 sectors, calling for a European Industrial Deal.
Translates Draghi into tools: simplification (−35% SME burden), the 28th regime, and digital sovereignty.
A key initiative cited as implementing Draghi's recommendations.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Innovation Gap & Productivity

blocks.t: Pillar 1 of the Compass — closing the innovation gap — is the first link between the new industrial strategy and digital policy. Europe’s competitiveness loss is attributed to its innovation gap, mostly in digital technologies.
The digital innovation-based GDP gap with the US widened over 20 years: from −17% in 2004 to −30% in 2023.

GDP/capita decomposition: GDP/capita = GDP/hour (productivity input) × hour/population (labour input). The productivity gap is far wider than the labour gap — about 72% of the per-capita gap is productivity, 28% labour. The productivity gap is largest in the ICT sector, which alone accounts for ~40% of the EU productivity gap.

Digital innovation-based productivity (share over time) — 1990: EU 27.4%, US 26.4%, China 1.6%, India 1.4%; 2019: EU 18.3%, US 22.9%, China 17%, India 3.3%; projected 2050: EU 11.3%, US 14.8%, China 20.4%, India 12.8%. The EU’s innovation-based productivity is declining in favour of emerging economies.

terms.d: Europe's competitiveness loss attributed mainly to a digital-technology innovation gap; the digital innovation-based GDP gap with the US widened from −17% (2004) to −30% (2023).
The EU-US per-capita gap is mostly productivity (~72%) not labour (~28%); ICT alone accounts for ~40% of the EU productivity gap.

quiz.source: This productivity gap is the most significant in the ICT sector, accounting for around 40% of the EU productivity gap.

quiz.source: 72% explained by the productivity gap (gdp/h) and 28% by labour gap (hours/capita).

sections.title: Deep Dive · What Is ‘Competitiveness’?

blocks.t: The Draghi Report does not define competitiveness, leaving great agency to the Commission and Member States to set the objective.

Two economic elements of competitiveness: (i) cost competitiveness — the product is cheaper; (ii) non-cost competitiveness — the product has a property that makes it better. Draghi’s definition appears wider, linking competitiveness to trade policy and strategic autonomy.

Prof. Lorenzani notes the wide definition can include non-cost competitiveness: even if the EU lags on pure cost, it may lead on quality, wellbeing and sustainability — financing wellbeing/sustainability to be a leader in values, even if no longer a GDP leader.
In nominal GDP, the 7 main emerging economies currently weigh ~66% of the G7’s GDP and are on track to exceed 100% of it.

terms.d: Cost: the product is cheaper. Non-cost: the product has a quality property that makes it better. Draghi's definition is wider, linking trade and strategic autonomy.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Competitiveness Compass — Pillars & Solutions

blocks.t: The Competitiveness Compass (Communication, November 2024) translates Draghi into policy and rests on his three pillars: (i) closing the innovation gap; (ii) a joint roadmap for decarbonisation and competitiveness (e.g. the Industrial Accelerator Act); (iii) reducing excessive dependencies and increasing security (e.g. a joint purchasing platform for CRM).

blocks.lead: The main initiatives serve five goals (the first two matter most):
items: Simplification — omnibus packages (CSRD, CS3D…).
Coordination — the 28th legal regime; common procurement for CRM.
Skills and quality jobs.

Financing opportunities — the Savings and Investment Union, going beyond the Capital Markets Union: a single capital market, plus financial literacy and mobilising private savings towards EU competitiveness (banks/insurers financing projects with European savings).
Refocused/streamlined EU budget and Semester.

blocks.t: One key initiative to close the innovation gap is the Start-up and Scale-up Strategy: improving SME financing, reducing regulatory fragmentation, and supporting access to public markets (and the 28th regime).

terms.d: A more ambitious successor to the Capital Markets Union: a single capital market plus financial literacy and mobilising private savings (banks/insurers) towards EU competitiveness.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Origins & Architecture of Foresight in the Commission

blocks.t: The first foresight unit in the Commission was created in 1987. In 1989, Jacques Delors created a ‘cellule de prospective’ close to the President — but it closed quickly and failed to embed foresight in policymaking.

VDL 1 changed this: she created a Commissioner for foresight (Maroš Šefčovič), taking over the Commission’s internal think tank (IDEA) and giving foresight real policy impact (e.g. the European Battery Alliance).

items: Political level: the Commissioner for foresight (a Vice-President) leading efforts to embed foresight.
Member-State level: foresight ministers (mostly EU-affairs ministers) in the EU Foresight Network of ‘Ministers of the Future’.
Administrative level: the Secretariat-General & JRC as lead services.
9 EU institutions in the inter-institutional network ESPAS.

blocks.t: The Strategic Foresight Network (2020) designates foresight contact points in each DG, diffusing foresight. Strategic foresight is therefore both top-down (Commissioner leadership) and bottom-up (socialisation via the ministers’ and DGs’ networks).

terms.d: A foresight cell created by Jacques Delors close to the Commission President; closed quickly and failed to embed foresight.
The Commission's internal think tank taken over by the foresight Commissioner (Šefčovič) under VDL 1.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Horizon-Scanning Protocol

blocks.lead: Inside the Commission, horizon scanning follows a protocol for short-term trends:
items: Scanners identify new ‘signs of change’ (e.g. de-dollarisation, a tree-extinction crisis).
A sense-making workshop of 15-20 people (the scanner community) analyses the signs to identify potential outcomes.
A synthesis of about 23 ‘weak signals of change’ is produced.
15-20 people from EU institutions analyse the weak signals in future-impact workshops…
…to predict future impacts of these weak signals on the EU.

blocks.t: Output: quarterly horizon-scanning newsletters presented to the College of Commissioners.

terms.d: A 15-20-person workshop in horizon scanning that analyses 'signs of change' to identify potential outcomes and produce 'weak signals'.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Competitiveness Coordination Tool (CCT)

items: Analytical work (including tech foresight) setting EU-wide competitiveness priorities.
Competitiveness dialogues and charters with all stakeholders (e.g. a plan after the wind dialogue).
Implementation via the European Semester, linking national actions/reforms to EU priorities.
Funding from the MFF (informing the EU Competitiveness Fund and the National Envelopes).

blocks.t: Problem: fragmentation at EU level — only 0.7% aggregate R&D expenditure, far below the US. The CCT aims to coordinate (rather than make compete) EU and national policies, simplify the budget/Semester, and refocus funding.

Pilot areas where the EU is still in the race: (i) energy & transport infrastructure (grids, sustainable fuels, batteries, charging); (ii) digital infrastructure & vertical AI use cases (AI Gigafactories); (iii) biotechnologies & key manufacturing (e.g. the Critical Medicines Act). Note: the CCT is not yet out.

terms.d: Coordinates EU and national competitiveness priorities via analytical work, dialogues/charters, the Semester and MFF funding; tackles fragmentation (only 0.7% aggregate R&D).
Cited as a CCT pilot area under biotechnologies and key manufacturing capacities.

quiz.q: EU fragmentation is shown by only ____% aggregate R&D expenditure, far below the US.
quiz.source: There is only 0.7% aggregate R&D expenditure in the EU, which is much less than for the USA.

quiz.source: Implementation (i.e. via European Semester) linking national actions and reforms to EU priorities.

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Strategic Foresight Reports, Year by Year

blocks.t: The common thread of all SFRs: strategic foresight should help the EU anticipate shocks, make long-term choices and make its policies more coherent. The content evolves with the political context — and the titles track the Commission’s shifting priorities.

items: 2020 — Resilience. The founding report (first annual SFR), triggered by COVID-19. Resilience is not a return to the status quo but the capacity to face, adapt and transform sustainably/justly/democratically — analysed across 4 dimensions: social-economic, geopolitical, green, digital. Announces the resilience dashboards.

2021 — Open strategic autonomy (the geopolitical dimension of resilience). Shifts from resilience to the EU’s capacity and freedom to act; identifies structural trends to 2050 (climate, hyperconnectivity, pressure on democracy, shifting world order, demography). ‘As open as possible, as autonomous as necessary.’

2022 — Twinning green + digital. The two transitions must not be treated separately — they can reinforce each other or create tensions (digital consumes much electricity/resources; e-waste; CRM dependence; cyber-risks). Focus sectors: energy, transport, industry, buildings, agriculture. Russia’s war is the geopolitical accelerator.

2023 — Sustainable competitiveness / wellbeing. Puts sustainability and people’s wellbeing at the heart of OSA: rise of ‘beyond GDP’, sustainable & inclusive wellbeing, a new social contract, intergenerational fairness. Proposes 10 areas for action.

2025 — ‘Resilience 2.0’ / preparedness. Reaction is no longer enough — the EU must be proactive, prepared, scenario-based (echoing the Niinistö report and the European Preparedness Union Strategy). A ‘Resilient EU 2040’ vision on three pillars: peace through European security; defence of democratic values; people’s wellbeing. Eight key areas for action.

blocks.t: The 2023 SFR measured competitiveness with health-adjusted GDP per capita: the EU would benefit most (+15.5%) vs the US/China (~+12%), helping close the gap.

sections.title: Deep Dive · Resilience Dashboards & the Granada Declaration

blocks.t: Resilience Dashboards: tables, based on the (mostly digital and geopolitical) megatrends the Commission monitors, that gauge the resilience of the EU and its Member States and their ability to progress toward objectives. They analyse four areas: (i) social & economic, (ii) green, (iii) digital, (iv) geopolitical. Produced since the 2020 SFR; since 2023 they are included in the European Semester Country Reports.

OSA was operationalised by the Spanish Presidency of the Council (2023) — the foresight ‘conveyor belt’ relies on the Council presidency. Spain (i) produced the foresight study ‘Resilient EU 2030’ with the Commission and a cluster of MS, and (ii) held the informal European Council of 6 October 2023, issuing the Granada Declaration on becoming more resilient and competitive in defence, industrial and digital policy.

The 10 OSA priorities include: resilient health & food systems; affordable decarbonised energy; capacity in data/AI/cutting-edge tech; securing/diversifying CRM supply; first-mover position in standard setting; resilient economic & financial systems; skills & talents; security, defence & space; working with global partners; and resilient institutions.

blocks.t: DG GROW mapped excessive dependencies across 11 sensitive industrial ecosystems: over-reliance on a limited number of actors for goods, services, data, infrastructures, skills and technologies, with limited internal capacity to substitute imports critical to the Union’s/MS’ strategic interests.

The EU is excessively reliant on Critical Raw Materials (CRM) given their economic importance and high supply risk — the weaponisation of dependencies has real effects: China’s export ban on germanium halted Germany’s car production.

blocks.lead: Obstacles to onshoring CRM extraction in the EU (resources exist but exploitation is slow and costly):
items: Lack of infrastructure.
Administrative burden / extraction-accreditation procedures (to be accelerated by the CRM Act).
Environmental constraints.
Social opposition (e.g. the Sami in Kiruna).

sections.title: Deep Dive · The Chips Market & EU Strategy

blocks.t: Not all chips are equal: many semiconductor types exist (optical, power, high-frequency…). AI chips differ from regular CPUs in computing power and type — AI chips use parallel computing (many tasks simultaneously) vs the sequential computing of regular chips (one task at a time).

State of the market: the EU has ~10% of world chip supply (−10 points vs 1990) and produces only 7% of wafers. Most chips are designed in one place and produced elsewhere: the US specialises in design (EDA & core IP) with little production; Taiwan and China together account for ~70% of production.

The EU strategy (Chips Act) is to specialise in strategic processors (AI and quantum chips) with the highest scalability — first-mover + first-to-scale captures the economies of scale. The April 2026 Chips Act aims to boost advanced microprocessor production (e.g. ASML in the NL), ‘from lab to fab’.

Debate: EU-only investment vs accepting FDIs (e.g. Intel opening a plant via FDI in Germany). The Commission is even considering an FDI screening based on competition — moving from ‘open DNA’ to ‘competition DNA’.

terms.d: Chips using parallel computing (many tasks at once), unlike regular CPUs that use sequential computing (one task at a time).
The Chips Act ambition to turn EU research into actual European foundry/manufacturing.
The Dutch firm cited in advanced microprocessor production capacity.

quiz.source: AI chips rely on parallel computing… while regular chips have sequential chips, operating one task at a time.

quiz.source: production… mostly operated in Taiwan and China, that mean 70% of the overall production.

sections.title: Deep Dive · Complexity, Relatedness & the Innovation Flywheel

blocks.t: Complexity: a technology that is difficult to develop/relocate confers a stronger comparative advantage (e.g. a cryptography system is harder to move than a solar plant). Relatedness: the potential for future specialisation — how likely a country is to move into a new technology given its existing skills and related sectors.

Strategically the EU should ask not only ‘what is complex?’ but ‘what is complex and related to what we already do well?’ The EU is specialised in low-complexity and green technologies (biotech, automotive) but weak in highly complex enabling tech (AI, quantum, cloud). It has a clear competitive advantage in only two fields: next-generation materials and the future of cleantech.
Example: China is more advanced in batteries, but the EU is highly related to batteries (skills + industrial base) — so by leveraging this it could gain a strategic advantage.
The innovation flywheel has three elements: knowledge, capital and scale.

terms.d: How hard a technology is to develop/relocate; complex technologies confer stronger comparative advantage.
The potential for future specialisation — how likely a country is to enter a new technology given its existing skills/sectors.
The three elements needed for innovation: knowledge, capital and scale.

options: the potential for future specialisation given existing skills/sectors
quiz.source: Relatedness potential for future specialization in some technologies.

quiz.q: The EU has a clear competitive advantage in only which two fields?
options: Next-generation materials and the future of cleantech
quiz.source: The EU only has a competitive advantage in two fields: next generation materials and future of cleantech.

quiz.q: The 'innovation flywheel' consists of…
quiz.source: 3 main elements to have innovation (the innovation flywheel): knowledge, capital and scale.

sections.title: Deep Dive · Capital — Public, Private & Competition Policy

blocks.t: The EU has abundant household savings but fails to channel them into productive investment in new technologies — hence a Commission push on financial literacy.

Public capital: on paper EU government R&D spending matches the US and China, but in reality the EU lags. China’s spending is underestimated (it invests via regional/local bodies and channels private spending through state-owned firms): China spends less but spends better. EU public spending is fragmented (mostly Member-State, no Single-Market perspective), and 90% of EU spending fails to achieve scale.

Competition law hinders scaling: state-aid rules limit scale, merger rules limit size. The Commission is reviewing when state aid can be granted without notification, to fund European champions — but not a total liberalisation (which would fragment the Single Market). Example: the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (simplifies aid for clean energy, lowers energy prices for energy-intensive industry, de-risks private investment via public guarantees).

Equity = investment as a share of a company (co-ownership): public equity (listed firms) and private equity (unlisted, riskier, mostly SMEs). Venture capital is private equity targeting innovative early-stage start-ups.

Private capital: risk/venture-capital funding in the EU is tiny — about 5%, vs the US 52% and China 40%. The EU relies on risk-averse bank financing (since the 2008 crisis). Draghi called for a publicly-controlled public equity fund. Cautionary example: in 2014 the German robotics firm Kuka was acquired by Chinese capital, hurting EU competitiveness and autonomy. sections.title: Deep Dive · Knowledge & Skills

blocks.t: Two indicators of knowledge/skills: (i) share of patent applications and (ii) distribution of top universities. Patents: the EU produces few but high-quality patents — 17% of world applications (US 21%, China 25%); the gap shrinks for high-quality patents (China boosts quantity, not quality).

Universities: most top-1000 universities (Shanghai ranking) are in the EU, but most of the top 10 are in the US/UK. Universities have spillover effects (e.g. Silicon Valley around Stanford); EU clusters (e.g. Paris) often specialise outside strategic tech (chemicals, beauty) — the middle technology trap.

items: National screening practices are too fragmented to mitigate technology leakage (the 4th pillar of the Economic Security Strategy targets R&D leakage; e.g. the Netherlands screens Chinese PhD applicants).
Only about 1/3 of EU patents are commercially exploited.
The EU fails to leverage its reverse dependencies (others’ dependence on the EU, e.g. quantum experts) because of brain drain.

blocks.t: Countermeasure: the ‘Choose Europe for Science’ initiative (May 2025) — values-driven research, high grants, high salaries and research freedom amid US pressure. A €900 million package attracted many foreign researchers in AI/quantum (e.g. Aix-Marseille University attracted 66+ foreign researchers in 2025).

sections.title: Deep Dive · Scale — Valley of Death & the Scale-up Trap

items: Complex, costly IP-filing procedures discouraging investors.
EU regulatory cost (precautionary principle vs innovation principle): ~100 tech laws and many national tech regulators — the EU should move toward the innovation principle.
Fragmentation across Member States.
A bad approach to competition policy (low state aid, restrictive mergers).
Scarce public-private partnerships in innovative procurement (IPCEIs are a failure).

blocks.t: Valley of death: the critical phase when a start-up has initial money to develop its technology but must industrialise and enter the market — costs explode while revenues stay uncertain, causing many bankruptcies. Scale-up trap (‘road to exile’): having survived with a product and customers, the firm needs venture capital/growth finance to scale — but EU late-stage funding is fragmented/insufficient (no European safe asset, incomplete CMU, little private equity), so firms leave for the US.
Result: EU firms are smaller than US ones; many SMEs, few new large firms. Only 8% of active unicorns in 2023 were from the EU (a unicorn = a company valued at ≥ €1 billion).

sections.title: Deep Dive · Export Controls, Wassenaar & Data Acts

blocks.t: The Wassenaar Arrangement (established 1996) is the multilateral regime for export controls. The US treats chips as key to China’s technological development and has imposed export-control measures.

blocks.lead: EU export controls could improve through:
items: Better targeting — you cannot simply stop GPU production (alternatives will emerge).
Better coordination — fewer, better-managed export controls (Member States applied them differently).

blocks.t: Submarine cables carry about $1 trillion of economic transactions per day; for ~10% of EU cable systems there is an espionage risk as China’s HMN is linked to Huawei. Under the new Digital Networks Act / Cybersecurity Act, Member States must phase out high-risk suppliers (ZTE and Huawei).
Two data laws to distinguish: the Data Act (governs public/industrial data access and sharing) and the Data Governance Act (framework for private data sharing).

terms.d: The multilateral export-control regime; the US uses chip export controls against China's tech development.

sections.title: Deep Dive · ‘Regulatory Un-peace’ & the Battle of Offers

blocks.t: Anu Bradford coined ‘regulatory un-peace’ — the tension between values and economic incentives in the horizontal battle between geo-blocks (US market-driven, China state-driven, EU rights-driven).

A battle of narratives can become a battle of offers: e.g. China’s Belt and Road Initiative comes bundled with the adoption of Chinese standards (China Standards 2035). Today about two-thirds of the world’s population live in countries that have taken a China/US stance.
The 2023 SFR called for creating regulatory alliances with well-chosen allies (a ‘transatlantic marketplace’, also in digital standards) to amplify the EU’s regulatory approach.

sections.title: Seminar (M. Havrda) · Foresight & Megatrends — Definitions

blocks.t: Foresight (Havrda): “a structured approach to presuming future developments based on historical development and current signals, in order to use the obtained knowledge for actions that may co-create the future (an active element).”
Megatrends (OECD): “relatively slow and certain directions of development, identified at the global level, and expected to change the face of the world substantially in the next decades.”
Strategic foresight is tightly linked to digitalisation precisely because digitalisation is itself a megatrend.
