flashcards.back: The global contest (2023 SFR) in which EU tech sovereignty competes with third-country propaganda and alternative offers (e.g. Belt and Road).
flashcards.concept: Battle of narratives, offers and models

flashcards.back: The EU's connectivity-investment offer, rivalled by China's Belt and Road / Digital Silk Road.
2023 risk-management approach: Promoting competitiveness, Protecting economic security, Partnering with like-minded countries (…and Preparing?).
Advanced chips, AI, quantum and biotech — flagged for immediate joint risk assessment.
Strategic Technologies for Europe Platform — vehicle under which support/restrictive measures for critical tech are evaluated.
Operationalises economic security via FDI screening, export-control coordination, outbound-investment screening and dual-use R&D; 6 high-risk areas tied to risk thresholds.
Governance framework with 2030 targets and DESI-based monitoring; MS produce 2-yearly Digital Decade Roadmaps.
Digital Economy and Society Index — the basis for Digital Decade annual monitoring reports.
EU Digital Infrastructure Consortia — vehicles for multi-country projects combining EU, MS and private investment (3 set up in 2024).
EU-wide cooperation on cybersecurity of critical infrastructure; harmonised requirements for essential and important entities; fines up to 2% of turnover.
Mandatory lifecycle cybersecurity requirements for manufacturers; CE marking; EU market access from 2027; fines up to €15mn or 2.5% turnover.
Voluntary EU cybersecurity certification scheme; security-by-design; permanent ENISA mandate; ECCC in Bucharest.
The EU Agency for Cybersecurity, given a permanent mandate by the Cybersecurity Act.
The use of supply/infrastructure dependencies (e.g. submarine cables) as leverage by third countries; a challenge to EU tech sovereignty.
The EU body for high-performance computing; 4 EU supercomputers are in the global top 10; amended to create AI factories.
AI factories (19 across 16 MS) open HPCs to startups to train trustworthy AI; the first 4–5 AI Gigafactories are planned for Europe.
Coordinates EU AI policies and implements the AI Act.
The next disruptive technology and a test for EU open strategic autonomy; could break current encryption; China leads, EU lags the 2030 target of 3 quantum computers.
The EU has lost the cloud market to US hyperscalers; competing head-on is unrealistic; a 'LEGO cloud' (e.g. Gaia-X) disappointed.
EU solutions (supported via public procurement) and local edge nodes that reduce hyperscaler dependence and keep data in the EU.
A European 'LEGO cloud' infrastructure initiative cited as having disappointed.
The umbrella linking AI Gigafactories, EU cloud/edge steps and related initiatives as part of the new digital industrial policy.
Influence via rules, values and standards rather than military/economic coercion.
The EU shapes global markets through regulation because firms adapt to EU rules and diffuse them beyond Europe.
China's assertive standard-setting strategy cited as a rival in the global 'battle of models'.
Anu Bradford's framing of three rival digital-governance models (US market-driven, China state-driven, EU rights-driven).
The horizontal battle for influence between geo-blocks over digital governance.
Horizontal = between geo-blocks (US/China/EU models); vertical = governments vs tech giants.
Trade and Technology Council moving towards a 'transatlantic marketplace'; ~half its working groups are digital/tech.
The EU achieving influence through true co-regulatory convergence in digital standardisation.
A controlled testing scheme under an experimentation clause; screens applicants, evaluates results before authorisation.
Technology for regulatory compliance (RegTech) and supervision (SupTech), used in implementation/enforcement.
An agenda-setting foresight tool working backwards from a desired future via transition pathways.
The UK FCA's 2016 sandbox (one of the first globally); influenced other jurisdictions alongside the EU's PSD2.
The EU's revised Payment Services Directive, part of the open-banking experience referenced in the sandbox example.
World's first horizontal AI regulation, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689; rights-based, risk-based, with agile tools (sandboxes, codes, guidance).
Voluntary industry pledges to anticipate AI Act provisions (100+ in Sep 2024, 230+ in Jan 2026).
Unacceptable (8 banned), high-risk (conformity assessment), low-risk (transparency), minimal (minimal obligations).
The strong compliance requirement imposed on high-risk AI systems.
General-purpose AI models; all face transparency requirements; high-impact ones presumed to pose systemic risks (notification, risk assessment, mitigation).
Up to EUR 35 million or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover (whichever higher) for the gravest infringements.
Under negotiation; extends AI Act compliance deadlines (02/12/27 for listed high-risk; 02/12/28 for AI in regulated products).
The EU project of integrating digital markets, reducing fragmentation and creating common rules for online services and digital business.
The combined green and digital transition; managing synergies and trade-offs between them over time.
The tension between competitiveness, decarbonisation, economic security (trilemma) plus fairness (quadrilemma) that industrial policy must manage (Renda, 2024).
Digital-enabled mobility models identified by the 2022 SFR to assuage green-digital trade-offs.
JRC scenarios of a sustainable Europe in 2050 along two axes: societal behaviour (individualistic vs collaborative) and policy mix (less vs more supportive of sustainability).
A 2050 scenario where market + innovation decouple profits from resource use (circular economy, renewables, bio-economy).
A 2050 scenario where, after failed policy responses to climate havoc, society adapts with lower material prosperity but stronger human relationships and community.
Links industrial transformation with human-centricity, sustainability and resilience.
A 'super-smart' society combining societal goals (SDGs) with new technologies.
EU-funded project that used HPC to screen molecules — a key AI/HPC use case for COVID-19 vaccines.
Whether the AI revolution causes job loss or job expansion; the goal is 'good jobs' in 'good sectors' via skills foresight (Renda, Balland, Bosoer 2023).
Anticipating skills needs across industrial ecosystems to empower workers and boost innovation.
80% of people with basic digital skills and 20 million ICT specialists by 2030; the EU currently lags both.
Adopted by the Council in October 2024; the EU is the first legislator worldwide to regulate platform work; MS have 2 years to transpose.
The Platform Work Directive's mechanism: workers presumed employees based on control/direction elements, unless rebutted; modalities set by each MS.
Cited as evidence of twinning mainstreaming across EU policymaking.
The 2025 strategy of which skills foresight and digital skills are a part.
Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 on online intermediary services: due-diligence obligations, systemic risks and platform accountability; protects users' fundamental rights, esp. vis-à-vis VLOPs.
Regulation imposing obligations on gatekeeper platforms to promote contestability and fairness; protects a level playing field for business users.
Very Large Online Platforms — the focus of the DSA's strongest obligations.
Large platforms subject to DMA obligations to ensure contestability and fairness.
The origin point for EU intermediary-liability and digital-services rules.
DSA obligations scale with the size and systemic role of the service; heaviest on VLOPs.
Mario Draghi's 2024 report on the future of European competitiveness; the course's central diagnosis of EU industrial-policy needs.
CEPS author of the 'North Star' industrial-policy paper, the Technology/Jobs Puzzle, the regulatory-tools policy-cycle map and IoT4SDGs.
A 1950s supranational defence framework (est. 1952), revisited by Fabbrini (2025) as a possible model for European defence solidarity.
EU leaders called Russia's war a 'tectonic shift in European history'.
Founded the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) by six countries.
A firm with no offshore production increasing national production that did not previously exist.
Bringing business operations set up abroad back to the domestic market (security, resilience, IP, quality, cost).
Producing in allied (like-minded) countries.
Locating production in directly neighbouring countries.
EU industrial policy swings cyclically between vertical (sector/champion-specific) and horizontal (economy-wide framework) models; VDL 1 accelerated the swing toward vertical.
(i) security/reduce dependencies; (ii) grow green technologies; (iii) close the innovation gap — with innovation-based productivity as the report's fil rouge.
Structural growth rests on demography and innovation; cyclical growth on short-term interest rates, shocks, trade and demand.
Signed by 1300+ business organisations across 25 sectors, calling for a European Industrial Deal.
Translates Draghi into tools: simplification (−35% SME burden), the 28th regime, and digital sovereignty.
A key initiative cited as implementing Draghi's recommendations.
Europe's competitiveness loss attributed mainly to a digital-technology innovation gap; the digital innovation-based GDP gap with the US widened from −17% (2004) to −30% (2023).
The EU-US per-capita gap is mostly productivity (~72%) not labour (~28%); ICT alone accounts for ~40% of the EU productivity gap.
Cost: the product is cheaper. Non-cost: the product has a quality property that makes it better. Draghi's definition is wider, linking trade and strategic autonomy.
A more ambitious successor to the Capital Markets Union: a single capital market plus financial literacy and mobilising private savings (banks/insurers) towards EU competitiveness.
Commission Communication translating Draghi's three pillars (close the innovation gap; decarbonisation+competitiveness; reduce dependencies+security) into policy.
A foresight cell created by Jacques Delors close to the Commission President; closed quickly and failed to embed foresight.
The Commission's internal think tank taken over by the foresight Commissioner (Šefčovič) under VDL 1.
Network designating foresight contact points in each DG; makes foresight both top-down and bottom-up.
A 15-20-person workshop in horizon scanning that analyses 'signs of change' to identify potential outcomes and produce 'weak signals'.
Cited as a CCT pilot area under biotechnologies and key manufacturing capacities.
First annual SFR; COVID-triggered; resilience as new compass across 4 dimensions (social-economic, geopolitical, green, digital).
Shift from reactive to proactive resilience/preparedness; 'Resilient EU 2040' vision (security, democratic values, wellbeing); links to the Niinistö report.
A 'beyond GDP' competitiveness measure used in the 2023 SFR; the EU would gain most (+15.5%).
Leaders' declaration from the 6 Oct 2023 informal European Council (Spanish Presidency) on resilience and competitiveness in defence, industrial and digital policy.
Materials of high economic importance and supply risk on which the EU is excessively dependent; subject to weaponisation (e.g. China's germanium ban).
Aims to accelerate the accreditation/permitting process for CRM extraction in the EU.
The Commission service that mapped excessive dependencies across 11 sensitive industrial ecosystems.
Chips using parallel computing (many tasks at once), unlike regular CPUs that use sequential computing (one task at a time).
The Chips Act ambition to turn EU research into actual European foundry/manufacturing.
The Dutch firm cited in advanced microprocessor production capacity.
How hard a technology is to develop/relocate; complex technologies confer stronger comparative advantage.
The potential for future specialisation — how likely a country is to enter a new technology given its existing skills/sectors.
The three elements needed for innovation: knowledge, capital and scale.
Public equity = shares of listed firms; private equity = shares of unlisted, riskier firms (mostly SMEs).
A type of private equity targeting innovative start-ups at an early stage; only ~5% in the EU vs 52% US, 40% China.

Other states' dependence on the EU (e.g. on EU quantum experts), under-leveraged because of brain drain.
A May 2025 initiative (~€900m) to attract researchers with grants, salaries and research freedom; e.g. Aix-Marseille attracted 66+ in 2025.
The phase when a start-up must industrialise and enter the market: costs explode, revenues uncertain, causing bankruptcies.
After the valley of death, EU firms lack late-stage venture/growth finance and leave for the US.
A company valued at ≥ €1 billion; only ~8% of 2023 active unicorns were from the EU.
A regulatory stance (vs the precautionary principle) the EU should adopt to become a digital regulatory power.
A €2-5bn EU fund directly investing in growing tech firms in strategic sectors to crowd in private capital.
An optional EU-wide legal regime for companies (non-binding uniform standards) reducing fragmentation; enables e.g. creating a company in 48 hours.
Upcoming act to close the EU cloud/AI infrastructure gap (data-centre efficiency, green data centres, AI Gigafactories, secure public-administration cloud).
2026 act implementing the 2025 Quantum Strategy: R&I, industrial capabilities, secure supply chains.
Regulation creating a Single Market for communications (5G, fibre, satellite, cloud); single authorisation, spectrum harmonisation; builds on the 2024 Gigabit Infrastructure Act.
The multilateral export-control regime; the US uses chip export controls against China's tech development.
